contentHtml:
New Delhi: Agra-based paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha has urged the Supreme Court to constitute an expert committee to examine gaps in the existing drug-pricing framework, arguing that the Centre's proposed price controls on selected anti-cancer medicines will not address the wider problem of overpriced medicines and hospital consumables.

Kulshrestha, who filed the original petition challenging exorbitant drug prices, submitted a rejoinder in response to an affidavit filed by the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers. While welcoming the government’s proposed intervention, he pointed out that none of the overpriced medicines cited in his petition belonged to the anti-cancer category.

In its affidavit before the Supreme Court, the Ministry stated that the Health Ministry had constituted an expert committee on October 9 to recommend anti-cancer drugs for price control, excluding inexpensive medicines. The Centre also projected that the maximum retail prices of affected medicines could decline by 20–70 per cent following the implementation of Trade Margin Rationalisation. Kulshrestha acknowledged the government’s decision to invoke Clause 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to reduce the prices of certain non-scheduled cancer medicines. However, he argued that restricting the intervention to cancer drugs would leave the broader problem of excessive mark-ups on other essential medicines unaddressed.

Referring to figures cited in the Ministry’s reply, Kulshrestha stated that ceiling prices had been fixed for only 935 of 3,881 new drugs, accounting for approximately 24 per cent. He argued that the remaining medicines did not have fixed ceiling prices and urged the government to exercise its powers under Clause 19 beyond anti-cancer medicines. He also questioned the Ministry’s apparent lack of concern about regulating low-priced drugs, stating that there was insufficient clarity regarding what constituted a “low-priced” medicine or the price threshold used to classify a drug in that category.

Kulshrestha maintained that affordable medicines benefit patients and argued that manufacturers, stockists and retailers generally determine their desired profits as a percentage, irrespective of the medicine’s price range. He further contended that retailers selling medicines across different price categories earn adequate profits on average. He sought clarification on the calculations used by the Centre to estimate a 20–70 per cent reduction in maximum retail prices and questioned how the government would establish that revised prices represented genuine and appropriate rates without leaving excessive or hidden profits for retailers. He called for a transparent mechanism for fixing the prices of all medicines and urged the proposed expert committee to document the methodology in its report to help identify deficiencies in the existing system and prevent further violations.

The Ministry had stated that hospitals purchase medicines from manufacturers offering the highest trade margins, reportedly ranging from 170 per cent to 700 per cent for anti-cancer drugs. It also argued that most major advances in medicine over the preceding 10–20 years had occurred in oncology, while prices in other therapeutic areas were comparatively lower. Kulshrestha described this explanation as “far from reality”, pointing out that healthcare involves more than 60,000 formulations derived from approximately 4,000 molecules.

According to Kulshrestha’s submission, the five leading drug categories in the Indian market by turnover are cardiac medicines, anti-diabetic drugs, antibiotics, medicines for gut acidity and painkillers. Anti-cancer medicines do not feature among these five categories. He further argued that newer medicines are emerging in other disease areas and that the Ministry should consider a broader range of drug categories for price regulation based on market turnover or therapeutic priority.

The Hindu BusinessLine reports that Kulshrestha has asked the Supreme Court to constitute an expert committee to examine loopholes in the existing drug-pricing mechanism and recommend appropriate corrective measures. He proposed that the committee include experts from the health and Goods and Services Tax (GST) departments to identify shortcomings in the pricing framework and develop measures to address excessive medicine prices. Kulshrestha maintained that price-control measures limited to anti-cancer drugs would not resolve the wider issue of excessive pricing across other therapeutic categories and hospital consumables.
